bug_description.original: A heap-buffer-overflow exists in the lexer, introduced in commit 87d05fb35ff9.
bug_description.normalized: In the staged vulnerable njs revision 6444ae6ab276f29e15abdd97cc3c865e3fa9c63d, the compiler initializes the lexer over the attacker-controlled 258-byte script buffer. The saved witness ends with a lone '?' byte at offset 257. `njs_lexer_next_token()` safely consumes that final byte under its outer `lexer->start < lexer->end` guard, advances `lexer->start` to the exclusive end pointer, classifies the byte as `NJS_TOKEN_CONDITIONAL`, and dispatches to `njs_lexer_multi()` to decide whether the token is '?' or '??'. Inside `njs_lexer_multi()`, the loop condition only checks `length != 0 && multi != NULL`; it never rechecks `lexer->start < lexer->end` before executing `c = lexer->start[0]`. That lookahead reads exactly 0 bytes to the right of the 258-byte heap input buffer, producing the observed AddressSanitizer `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` in `njs_lexer_multi`. The fix commit 3313d0d593a09f27b7aab54c70dc808c61021ac5 adds the missing `lexer->start < lexer->end` predicate to that loop and adds regression tests for EOF token prefixes such as `>`, `>>`, `>>>`, `==`, and `?`.

source.description: First project statement that materializes the attacker-controlled script span into lexer state. `njs_vm_compile()` hands the current script pointer and exclusive end pointer into `njs_lexer_init()`, which seeds the `lexer->start` and `lexer->end` bounds later misused by the multi-token matcher.
source.value_from: In the libFuzzer entry `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` (`src/njs_shell.c:592-595`), the harness sets `script.length = size; script.start = (u_char *) data;` and calls `njs_process_script(&opts, vm_options.external, &script)`. The staged PoC is the exact 258-byte file `gt_results/arvo_20905/poc` (sha256 `5387eabd70962f54baefe133a4af8b8802c599ac896a0da88cc8cb5b46b260c7`), whose final byte at offset 257 is `0x3f` ('?').

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. After the final '?' has already advanced `lexer->start` to the exclusive buffer end, this lookahead reads one byte at `lexer->end`, i.e. the first byte past the 258-byte heap buffer loaded from the saved PoC.
sink.note: The staged ASan trace reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` at `src/njs_lexer.c:868:13` and says the faulting address is 0 bytes to the right of a 258-byte region.

root_cause.description: Missing end-of-buffer guard. `njs_lexer_multi()` enters its lookahead loop based only on remaining token-table candidates and never proves `lexer->start < lexer->end` before reading another byte from the script buffer.
root_cause.note: When the current token is the final '?' in the witness, step 4 has already advanced `lexer->start` to `lexer->end`, but this loop still executes once more. The upstream fix adds `&& lexer->start < lexer->end` to this condition.

tainted_value_origin.description: The vulnerability-relevant attacker-controlled value is the final script byte '?'. `njs_lexer_next_token()` reads that last byte under the outer in-bounds guard and advances `lexer->start` to exactly `lexer->end`, creating the EOF state mishandled by `njs_lexer_multi()`.

parser_admitted.description: The saved fuzz buffer has already been accepted as njs source text and `njs_process_script()` now hands its full `(start, end)` span to the compiler, entering project lexing on the 258-byte witness.

coarse_trace.summary: The compiler entry point receives the 258-byte staged script and invokes `njs_vm_compile()` on its full `(start, end)` span.
Compilation initializes `lexer->start` and `lexer->end` over the attacker-controlled heap buffer so later tokenization can walk from the first byte to the exclusive end pointer.
While parsing an expression, the parser performs lookahead and asks the lexer to produce another token from the remaining script tail.
The lexer consumes the witness's final '?' byte, advances its cursor to the exclusive end pointer, classifies the byte as `NJS_TOKEN_CONDITIONAL`, and dispatches to the multi-token matcher.
The multi-character token matcher omits an end-of-buffer guard and performs a one-byte lookahead at `lexer->end`, matching the saved ASan heap-buffer-overflow READ.

fine_trace.note: Source. `njs_vm_compile()` passes the attacker-controlled script pointer and exclusive end pointer into the lexer initializer. For the staged witness, this span is the 258-byte heap buffer loaded from `gt_results/arvo_20905/poc`.
Stores the current lexer cursor at the first byte of the attacker-controlled script buffer.

Stores the exclusive upper bound of the same script buffer. For the staged PoC this bound is exactly 258 bytes after `start`, matching ASan's report that the invalid read happened 0 bytes past a 258-byte region.

After earlier tokens advance through the witness, the final lexer iteration reaches the last byte `?` at offset 257. The outer `while (lexer->start < lexer->end)` guard admits this in-bounds read, and the post-increment moves `lexer->start` to exactly `lexer->end`.
Classifies the consumed byte `?` as `NJS_TOKEN_CONDITIONAL`, selecting the lexer path that distinguishes a lone `?` from the multi-character `??` token.

Because `token->type` is `NJS_TOKEN_CONDITIONAL`, the lexer calls `njs_lexer_multi()` with the conditional-token table `{{ '?', NJS_TOKEN_COALESCE, 0, NULL }}` and `length == 1`, i.e. a single-byte lookahead candidate beyond the already consumed `?`.

Root cause. The multi-token loop checks only the token-table cursor and remaining candidate count; it does not recheck `lexer->start < lexer->end`. After step 4, `lexer->start` already equals the exclusive bound from step 3, but this loop still executes once more on the final `?`.

Sink. With `lexer->start == lexer->end`, this one-byte lookahead reads the first byte past the 258-byte heap input buffer. The saved ASan trace reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` at this statement and says the faulting address is 0 bytes to the right of the input region.

allocation_context.note: ASan reports the invalid read is 0 bytes to the right of a 258-byte heap region allocated by the AFL/libFuzzer driver when it loaded the staged PoC.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: staged sanitizer_trace.txt and reproduction_report.json; fixed image was not dynamically validated in Stage 02

poc.trigger: Stage 01's saved vulnerable run executed `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_20905 run --version vulnerable --expect crash`, which fed `poc` to `njs_process_script_fuzzer` and reproduced `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` in `njs_lexer_multi` with stack `njs_lexer_next_token -> njs_lexer_token_push`.

format.name: njs JavaScript source text
format.contract: Exactly the 258-byte witness stored in `gt_results/arvo_20905/poc` (sha256 `5387eabd70962f54baefe133a4af8b8802c599ac896a0da88cc8cb5b46b260c7`). The crash-relevant property is that the final byte at offset 257 is a lone `?`, so when lexing reaches that byte `njs_lexer_next_token()` reads it under `lexer->start < lexer->end`, advances `lexer->start` to the exclusive end pointer, classifies it as `NJS_TOKEN_CONDITIONAL`, and immediately asks `njs_lexer_multi()` to look one byte farther for `??`. That EOF `?` condition is what makes the saved run perform the out-of-bounds lookahead at `lexer->end`.
